content: The World Health Organization (WHO) developed a set of initial questions to guide the creation of a guideline on sugar intake for adults and children. These questions were designed to address the needs of Member States and international partners for policy and program guidance. The Population, Intervention, Comparison, and Outcome (PICO) format was used to structure these questions. The PICO questions were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat and the WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guideline Development and were subsequently made available for public comment in February 2010. Feedback was received from 16 individuals and organizational stakeholders, and the questions were revised as necessary. The draft PICO questions were presented to the Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG) Subgroup on Diet and Health during its first meeting in February 2010. At this meeting, the guideline topic was introduced, the scope of the guideline and the PICO questions were discussed, and the importance of outcomes and populations was ranked by NUGAG members. The prioritization of the PICO questions defined the scope of the evidence to be used in developing the guideline. Following the meeting, WHO commissioned several systematic reviews and meta-analyses to address the PICO questions. During the February 2010 NUGAG meeting, challenges in identifying sufficient data on weight gain, particularly from developing countries, were discussed. To address this limitation, NUGAG members from developing countries offered to share available country data. Additionally, in August 2010, WHO issued a call for data to all countries through its regional offices to systematically collect the best available data and evidence from developing countries. However, no data met the inclusion criteria outlined in the PICO questions. A follow-up meeting of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health was held in March 2011, during which preliminary outcomes of the systematic reviews were discussed. At this meeting, NUGAG members requested further analyses, including the preparation of GRADE evidence profiles, which had not been included in the initial reviews. Subsequent meetings were held in November–December 2011, March 2012, and March 2013, during which the evidence and GRADE assessments were reviewed and discussed. The draft recommendations were finalized through consensus among NUGAG members and the WHO Secretariat. There were no significant disagreements among NUGAG members regarding any aspect of the guideline. In accordance with WHO's rules, all experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before participating. These declarations were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat in consultation with the WHO Legal Office. Additionally, participants verbally declared their interests at the start of each meeting. The procedures for managing conflicts of interest outlined in WHO's guidelines were strictly followed. Summaries of declared interests from NUGAG members, external resource persons, and external peer reviewers are provided in Annex 8. Two systematic reviews were commissioned to assess the effects of increasing or decreasing free sugar intake on two critical health outcomes: excess weight gain and dental caries. Initially, other outcomes, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease (CVD), were considered. However, after extensive discussions, it was decided that excess weight gain and dental caries should be the primary outcomes of concern in relation to free sugar intake. The risk of developing type 2 diabetes and CVD is often mediated through the effects of overweight and obesity, among other risk factors. Therefore, measures aimed at reducing overweight and obesity are likely to also reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes and CVD, as well as their associated complications. The systematic review on body weight examined the effects of free sugar intake on excess adiposity in adults and children. It also evaluated whether current evidence supports the existing recommendation to reduce free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake. Body weight was selected as an outcome due to the significant contribution of obesity-related comorbidities to the global burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Studies included in the review involved interventions advising changes in free sugar intake without emphasizing weight loss. Trials specifically designed to achieve weight loss were excluded. The evidence for changes in body weight in adults related to both increasing and decreasing free sugar intake was considered moderate in quality, while the evidence for children was also moderate for reductions in sugar intake but low for increases in sugar intake. The systematic review on dental caries addressed the relationship between free sugar intake and dental caries in adults and children. The evidence suggested a positive association between the amount of free sugar intake and dental caries in both children and adults. The quality of evidence for dental caries was generated from eight cohort studies, with seven of these studies reporting higher dental caries with higher sugar intake. The studies also indicated that lower levels of dental caries were observed when free sugar intake was less than 10% of total energy intake compared to levels above 10%. However, the data from these studies were not suitable for pooling due to variability in how the data were reported. WHO recommends reducing free sugar intake throughout the life course. Specifically, it recommends reducing free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake in both adults and children.
